title: Novel and potent MICA/B antibody is therapeutically effective in KRAS LKB1 mutant lung cancer models
author: Ryan R Kowash; Manoj Sabnani; Laura T Gray; Qing Deng; Nusrat U A Saleh; Luc Girard; Yujiro Naito; Kentaro Masahiro; John D Minna; David E Gerber; Shohei Koyama; Zhiqian Lucy Liu; Hemanta Baruah; Esra A Akbay
text:
Abstract
Background
Concurrent KRAS LKB1 (STK11, KL) mutant non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) do not respond well to current immune checkpoint blockade therapies, however targeting major histocompatibility complex class I-related chain A or B (MICA/B), could pose an alternative therapeutic strategy through activation of natural killer (NK) cells.
Methods
Expression of NK cell activating ligands in NSCLC cell line and patient data were analyzed. Cell surface expression of MICA/B in NSCLC cell lines was determined through flow cytometry while ligand shedding in both patient blood and cell lines was determined through ELISA. We engineered an antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) enhanced MICA/B monoclonal antibody, AHA-1031, which prevents ligand shedding without interfering with binding to natural killer group 2D while targeting cancer cells via superior ADCC. We performed in vitro assays using ELISA and flow cytometry-based assays to confirm that our antibody potently binds to and stabilizes MICA/B expression across lung cancer and other solid tumor cell lines. Additionally, we used two KL mutant NSCLC cell lines and a KL mutant patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model to demonstrate in vivo antitumor efficacy and flow cytometry analysis for immune cell activation profiling.
Results
NSCLC cell lines exhibit high MICA/B expression and secrete soluble MICA/B in vitro. Soluble MICA/B is also detected in patient blood samples. AHA-1031 binds to the α3 domain of MICA/B, preventing shedding and targeting tumor cells to ADCC. AHA-1031 exhibits high affinity and specificity to MICA/B, preventing MICA/B shedding in tumor lines and inducing ADCC in vitro. Our antibody also effectively binds and stabilizes MICA/B expression in additional tumor types and demonstrates broad specificity. We show that in two KL mutant NSCLC xenograft models and a KL mutant PDX model, treatment with AHA-1031 monotherapy significantly inhibits tumor growth compared with vehicle-treated animals with no observable toxicity. Tumor tissues from treated mice exhibit significantly increased immune cell infiltrates and activated NK cell populations.
Conclusions
Activating NK cells through MICA/B stabilization and inducing ADCC offers an alternative and potent therapy option in KL tumors. MICA/B are shed across different tumors making this therapeutic strategy universally applicable.
Keywords: Natural killer - NK, Lung Cancer, Antibody, MICB antigen, MHC class I-related chain A
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC
KL mutant non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) has proved incredibly difficult to treat. High levels of shed major histocompatibility complex class I-related chain A or B (MICA/B) are known to inhibit natural killer (NK) cells and promote evasion of innate immunity. Therefore, this study strived to determine whether the stabilization and prevention of shedding of MICA/B with a novel antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)-enhanced antibody could overcome current limitations with T-cell activating therapies.
WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS
This study demonstrates that a novel MICA/B monoclonal antibody, which binds and prevents shedding of this ligand, while also inducing ADCC is effective in preclinical models of KL mutant NSCLC. ADCC improved IgG1-Fc engineered antibody, AHA-1031, is significantly more effective than its corresponding antibody, AHA-1032, with a wild-type IgG1-Fc.
HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY
Our study highlights the critical need to explore NK cell activating therapies and we make the case that our novel antibody could provide an added therapeutic benefit especially in tumor types that do not respond well to immune checkpoint blockade therapy.
Background
Natural killer (NK) cells play a key role in the host innate immune responses, protecting from pathogens and cancer.1 NK cells are particularly important for preventing lung cancer as depletion of NK cells in genetically engineered models of lung adenocarcinoma was reported to increase tumor formation.2 Unlike T cells which require major histocompatibility complex (MHC) for tumor cell recognition and cytotoxic effect, NK cells rely on a complex interplay of both inhibitory and activating ligand-receptor interactions.3 4 In humans NK cell activating ligands include MHC class I-related chain A or B (MICA/B) and the UL16 binding proteins (ULBP1-6).5 Their engagement to the natural killer group 2D (NKG2D) activating receptor, expressed on NK cells and T-cell subsets, results in activation of these immune cell populations.3 However, there are numerous mechanisms that tumor cells use to avoid immune detection. One of these mechanisms is the shedding of MICA/B ligands which limit NK and T-cell binding to tumor cells leading to decreased immune cell activation.6 7 Thus, the dual function of an antibody that binds to and prevents the release of these ligands from target cancer cells, thereby re-engaging the activating NKG2D receptor found on NK cells and certain T-cell subsets—alongside antibody-mediated cell-dependent cytotoxicity (ADCC), has recently gained attention as a promising therapeutic strategy.
MICA/B are stress-induced ligands and are highly expressed in numerous cancer types including melanoma, glioma, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).8,10 However, proteases within the tumor microenvironment can cleave these ligands resulting in reduced expression on tumor cells.11 12 Soluble MICA/B in the blood has been detected in patients with various cancer types and serum levels are thought to correlate with disease progression which was also demonstrated in patients with NSCLC.8 13 14 NSCLC is the most common form of lung cancer accounting for around 85% of all lung cancer cases and affecting hundreds of thousands of patients in the USA every year. Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) is the current standard of care for NSCLC.15 However, response rates for some subsets of lung cancer remain low and resistance to current therapies is a major challenge.16 Therefore, the development of new therapies that overcome current limitations is needed.
The mutational landscape of NSCLC comprises common cancer drivers such as KRAS and EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) and loss of tumor suppressors TP53 and LKB1 (STK11).17 18 KRAS is mutated in 30–40% of lung adenocarcinomas and among those about one-third of them have inactivating mutations in STK11. Concurrent KRAS and LKB1 mutant (KL) NSCLCs are especially difficult to treat, express low PD-L1, present T-cell exclusion and do not respond well to ICB therapy.19,21 This underlines the critical need to develop new immunotherapies for this subset of lung cancers.
To develop an alternative immune activating mechanism, we developed an MICA/B antibody AHA-1032, our initial lead candidate with a WT IgG1-Fc region, followed by AHA-1031 with an engineered IgG1-Fc region, that both target MICA/B resulting in a potent effect on NK cell activation. Of note, like AHA-1031, anti-MICA/B antibody 7C6 was previously reported to bind the α3 domain of MICA/B, preventing their proteolytic cleavage from the cancer cell surface and thereby increasing ligand presence on the cell surface.7 This facilitates the interaction with the NKG2D on NK cells, as well as a subset of T cells including γδ T cells, NKT cells, and CD8+T cells. 7C6 demonstrated promising in vitro activity and in vivo tumor inhibition capability by facilitating the interaction of MICA with NKG2D and promoting ADCC. Interestingly the tumor inhibition ability of 7C6 was reduced for 7C6-DANA analog.7 22 DANA mutations result in the abolishment of IgG1-Fc binding to CD16a suggesting ADCC-mediated cell killing remains a crucial path for tumor inhibition. It is important to note that 7C6, CLN-619 and DM919 (anti-MICA/B antibodies currently in phase I clinical trial (NCT05117476 and NCT06328673)), and our antibodies AHA-1032 and AHA-1031 all bind to the alpha 3 domain of MICA/B and prevent shedding. Importantly AHA-1031 differs from these antibodies through the incorporation of an engineered human IgG1 Fc to enhance ADCC function. To enhance the binding of IgG1-Fc to CD16a in AHA-1032, we introduced mutations known to increase ADCC activity23 to yield AHA-1031.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate NK cell activating therapy agents specifically in KL mutant NSCLC, revealing that effectively engaging multiple potent NK activating receptors enhances NK cell cytotoxicity. We focused our study on KL mutant NSCLC tumors due to current treatment ineffectiveness, yet our method is potentially widely applicable to other subtypes of NSCLC or other cancers as MICA/B are widely expressed.
Materials and methods
Expression analysis
Previously published NSCLC cell line24 and patient tumor25 gene expression data were downloaded and analyzed. Proteomics data was acquired from a previously published study26 and analyzed.
Flow cytometry
Cells were stained with fixative live dead cell stain (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 50-112-1528) for 8 min at room temperature. Cells were then stained with fluorophore-conjugated antibodies in Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) buffer (2% Fetal bovine serum (FBS) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 20 min on ice. Tissue samples were digested for 30 min at 37°C with 100 units/mL collagenase type IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 17104019) 10 µg/mL DNAase I (Sigma catalog number DN25), and 10% heat-inactivated FBS in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) media to disassociate cells. Red blood cells were lysed with ACK lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no A1049201). Tissues were filtered through a 70 µm cell strainer to make single-cell suspension. Cells were stained with fixative live dead cell stain followed by CD16/32 antibody (BioLegend, catalog no. 101320) for 20 min on ice. Next, they were incubated with fluorophore-conjugated antibodies. Intracellular staining was performed by eBioscience Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog no. 00-5523-00) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. To determine NK cell activation, lymphocytes were enriched using Ficoll-Paque (GE HealthCare, catalog no. GE17-5446-02) following the protocol. Enriched samples were incubated with Phorbol 12-Myristate 13-Acetate (PMA)/ionomycin/GolgiPlug for ex vivo stimulation for 6 hours. The same staining protocol as detailed above was used. Samples were run on BD FACSCanto or Attune NxT (Thermo Scientific), and flow data were analyzed using FlowJo.
Antibody production
Production of recombinant antibodies was conducted either in EXPI293 cells or outsourced to WuXi Biologics, where it was produced in CHO-K1 cells. The process involved using two plasmids, one encoding the light chain (pcDNA 3.1 LC) and the other encoding the heavy chain (pcDNA 3.1 HC). For EXPI293 production, these plasmids were co-transfected into EXPI293F suspension cells using lipid-based ExpiFectamine 293 Transfection Kit (catalog no. A14525, Thermo Fisher Scientific) per the kit’s instructions. Transfected cells were cultured at 37°C with 8% CO2 and 120 rpm. After 5–6 days post-transfection, supernatants underwent protein affinity purification using a high-performance 5 mL HiTrap MabSelect SuRe column (Cytiva, catalog no. 11003494) from GE Healthcare Life Sciences for large-scale production.
Shedding inhibition of MICA on cancer cell surface by alpha 3 domain-specific MICA antibodies (ELISA-based assays)
Human cell lines A375 (CRL-1619), Calu3 (HTB-55), PANC1 (CRL-1469), Capan2 (HTB-80), OVACAR3 (HTB-161), HCT116 (CCL-247), 22Rv1 (CRL-2505), and PC3 (CRL-1435) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (USA) and A549 (CCL-185), and H2030 (CRL-5914) were obtained from the Hamon Center for Therapeutic Oncology. All cell lines were cultured in their recommended media with 1% antibiotic mixture (penicillin/streptomycin—Pen/Strep, 10,000 IU/mL; Sigma-Aldrich) and 10% fetal bovine serum. The cells were maintained at 37°C in humidified incubators containing 5% CO2.
Tumor cells were cultured with our α3 domain-specific anti-MICA antibodies and control benchmark antibodies (including Hu Isotype IgG1 and cell-only group) for 24–72 hours in cell-culture treated 96-well plates. Supernatants were harvested and MICA and MICB levels were quantified via sandwich ELISA (R&D Systems, DY1300 and DY1599).
Isolation of NK cells from donor PBMCs (peripheral blood mononuclear cells)
Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated via Ficoll-Paque gradient centrifugation, employing products from Amersham Pharmacia Biotech (Uppsala, Sweden), using buffy coat obtained from Carter BloodCare (Bedford, Texas, USA). Human primary NK cells were isolated from the cryopreserved PBMCs using the NK Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, catalog no. 130-092-657) per the manufacturer’s instructions.
Antibody-dependent cytotoxicity assays
ADCC activity of human primary NK cells was evaluated using a two-color flow cytometric assay.27 Target tumor cells (1×106) were incubated with carboxyfluorescein diacetate succinimidyl ester (CFSE; Invitrogen, Eugene, Oregon, USA) in PBS for 10 min at 37°C. Target cells were washed thrice with ice-cold RPMI 1640 medium. NK cells were mixed with target cells at indicated ratios and incubated with antibodies overnight. Cells were washed twice with PBS and stained with 7-aminoactinomycin D (7-AAD; eBioscience, San Diego, California, USA) for analysis via two-color flow cytometry, conducted on an Attune device (Thermo Scientific). CFSE and 7-AAD double-positive cells were considered “lysed cells”. The EC50 was calculated using non-linear regression analysis.
MICA/B ELISA of patient blood and cell lines
Cells were plated in a 6-well plate at a density of 0.5 million/well and cultured in a complete growth medium. Cell culture media were collected 48 hours later and centrifuged at 1,500 rpm for 10 min at 4°C to collect the supernatant. MICA/B concentration was determined using human MICA and MICB ELISA kits as above.
Patient tumor volumes were calculated based on the sum of the diameters of target lesions, including primary tumors and metastatic tumors, according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST, V.1.1). The objective response was evaluated at 6 weeks after treatment and every 6 weeks thereafter. Responders were defined as PR (partial response) or SD (stable disease), and non-responders as PD (progressive disease) at 3 months (6 cycles × 2 weeks) after initiation of nivolumab treatment. Patient characteristics are detailed in online supplemental figure 1. MICA/B levels in blood were determined using the ELISA kits mentioned above.
Mouse xenograft and patient-derived xenograft models
All mouse experiments were performed following the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and ARRIVE guidelines. Mice were housed in standard IACUC recommended conditions. 5 million A549 or H2030 (in 50% matrigel (Corning, catalog no. 354230) were implanted into 4–8 weeks old athymic nude mice (The Jackson Laboratory, catalog no. 002019). LTL-657 patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model was obtained from the Hamon Center and tumors were generated by implanting pieces of tumors into the flanks of nude mice. Male and female mice were used for cell line experiments and only female mice were used for PDX experiments. Treatments were initiated when tumors reached 75–100 mm3. Mice were evenly distributed into vehicle or treatment groups based on tumor volumes and gender/where applicable. Vehicle (PBS) or 10 mg/kg AHA-1031 were administered by Intraperitoneal (IP) injections. Tumors were measured with a digital caliper and tumor volumes were calculated using the formula=width (mm)×width (mm)×length (mm)/2.
B16F10 metastasis experiments
B16F10 cells were transduced with lentiviral vector pLvX-EF1a-MICA-IRES-puro. After MICA expression was validated by flow cytometry, C57BL/6 mice were injected with 1 million B16F10-MICA cells by intravenously. Male and female mice were randomized and distributed into control and treatment groups. Mice were treated with either vehicle or AHA-1031 (200 µg per dose) IP on indicated days. Mice were euthanatized at the end point and lungs were isolated and fixed in formalin.
ELISA for Cytokine Release Analysis in Human PBMCs
PBMCs were incubated in media with isotype control, AHA-1031, or CD3-CD28 antibodies at 37°C overnight. Supernatants were collected for flow-based multiplexing and cytokines were quantified according to the manufacturer’s instructions (BioLegend catalog no. 740930).
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were completed with GraphPad Prism software. P values were determined using single or multiple unpaired two-tailed t-tests for analysis unless otherwise noted. Significant p values are shown as: *p<0.05,∗∗p<0.01, ∗∗∗p<0.001, ∗∗∗∗p<0.0001.
Data availability statement
Publicly available data sets were used for the analysis of cell line and tumor gene expression24 25 and proteomics.26 Data from the antibody screen is available from the corresponding authors on reasonable request.
Results
NSCLCs express and shed MICA and MICB proteins
We analyzed the expression of all NKG2DLs- MICA, MICB, and ULBP1-6 in lung adenocarcinoma (LuAd) cell lines and primary patient tissue samples from the lung cancer genome atlas (TCGA) data set.24 25 MICA/B and ULBP1-3 are highly expressed while ULBP4-6 are expressed at lower levels (figure 1A,B). MICA is the highest expressed NKG2D ligand in LuAds both for cell lines and tumor tissue at the RNA level. We also observed that five of the seven KL mutant LuAD cell lines express higher levels of MICA compared with the mean of all LuAd cell lines and express other NKG2D ligands within the mean range of all LuAd cell lines suggesting that targeting MICA/B within this subset is reasonable (figure 1A). Consistent with the cell lines, KL mutant LuAd tumors expressed MICA at the highest level among all NKG2DLs (online supplemental figure 1A). Previous reports suggest that KL mutant lung tumors have reduced expression of genes involved in antigen presentation,28 highlighting the potential significance of NKG2DL expression. We had previously shown that LuAds also shed these ligands.9 We validated this using a data set comprising a large cohort of 1,400 blood samples from patients with common cancer types.26 These included lung cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, ovarian cancer, endometrial cancer, prostate cancer, glioma, and hematological cancers-myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and lymphoma . This data set included blood samples from 268 patients with lung cancer. In this proteomics-based assay, MICA/B were elevated in the blood of the majority of patients from all cancers in this data set (figure 1C).
We next validated this in an independent cohort of patient samples from Osaka University where we had information about patients’ response to nivolumab. There was no difference in the characteristics of the patients in responder or non-responder cohorts (online supplemental figure 1B). Response to nivolumab was determined based on RECIST criteria for primary tumors and metastatic tumors. The objective response was evaluated at 6 weeks after treatment and was repeated every 6 weeks thereafter. Responders (=sensitive) were defined as PR or SD, and non-responders (=resistance) as PD at 3 months (6 cycles every 2 weeks) after initiation of nivolumab treatment (online supplemental figure 1B). Consistent with the large data set, patients with NSCLC had MICA and MICB expression in their blood as determined by ELISA. We previously showed that MICA is undetectable in most of the blood samples in healthy individuals.9 We did not see a significant difference in MICA levels in responders as compared with non-responders, but MICB levels were much higher in patients who responded to nivolumab treatment (figure 1D). Interestingly, levels of shed MICB were higher than MICA which has been reported previously in another cancer type.29
To determine expression levels of MICA/B specifically in the models used in this study, we first confirmed tumor cell surface expression in KL lines A549 and H2030 by flow cytometry. H2030 has additionally TP53 mutation. Consistent with RNA, these cells expressed elevated levels of MICA/B. In contrast, a small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) cell line H69 did not express surface MICA/B as expected (figure 1E). These two lines also shed MICA into the media and levels of soluble MICA in the media correlated with their cell surface expression whereas SCLC cell line H69 with no surface MICA/B expression did not shed MICA (figure 1F).
Discovery and development of alpha 3 domain-specific MICA/B specific antibodies
To develop our novel antibodies, we used Alloy Therapeutics’ (ATX-Gx) proprietary transgenic mouse platform to generate fully human anti-MICA/B antibodies. Alpha 3 truncated domains of MICA or MICB and both monovalent and bivalent forms of human and cynomolgus (cyno) MICA or MICB were used as immunogens to raise antibodies. This strategy maximizes the probability of enriching antibodies that bind to the desired epitope with cyno MICA cross reactivity. We applied a three-prong antibody discovery strategy (phage display, yeast display, and B-cell platform) and thereby cast a wide net to identify potentially best-in-class antibodies.
We produced a total of 54 antibodies in the EXPI293 expression platform. Dissociation constant (KD) measurements were performed for all the 54 purified antibodies by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) against human full-length MICA, MICB, the alpha 3 domain of MICA and MICB. Briefly, all 54 clones bind to full-length human MICA, 41 clones bind to the desired alpha 3 domain of both human MICA and MICB, 33 of those 41 monoclonal antibodies (mAb)s cross react with the alpha 3 domain of cynomolgus MICA (figure 1G and online supplemental figure 2A). We next performed cell binding of the 54 antibodies to confirm that the antibodies that bind to recombinant antigens are also able to bind MICA expressed on the cell surface. More than 80% of the antibodies bind specifically to MICA overexpressing Raji cells compared with parental Raji cells (figure 1G). We also performed extensive binning analysis by SPR and identified as many as six different binning epitopes. This diversity in binding epitope allowed us to identify multiple mAbs with the right biology and developability profiles. Size-exclusion chromatography profiles for all 54 purified antibodies were acquired before and after freeze thaw. The thermal stability of the antibodies was assessed via nano differential scanning fluorimetry and was in a similar range to that of clinical antibodies (figure 1H). As a second step based on clonotype, affinity, epitope and developability properties, we narrowed down from 54 to 26 clones. We subsequently ran in vitro assays to identify antibodies that are most efficient in blocking the proteolytic cleavage of MICA from the cancer cell surface. We monitored the cleavage inhibition efficiency by two independent methods using A375 melanoma cells as a standard cancer cell line: (1) a FACS-based protocol, where an increase in fluorescence intensity on overnight incubation with antibodies indicates stabilization of surface MICA expression, and (2) an ELISA-based protocol, where overnight incubation of A375 cells with anti-MICA antibodies result in the depletion of cleaved soluble MICA in the cell culture media.
Additionally, we performed multiple developability assays including binding to baculovirus particles, soluble membrane preparations, single-stranded DNA, insulin, and affinity-capture self-interaction nanoparticle spectroscopy (online supplemental figure 2B). Moreover, we conducted an early assessment of the clinical utility potential of the germlines of our antibodies and immunogenicity profiling using two methods: Humanness and T20 scores, comparing them to nivolumab, discovered using a similar transgenic mouse platform. Our four lead candidates exhibit features like Food and Drug Administration-approved antibodies, providing confidence for further development (online supplemental figure 2C,D). Out of the four candidates, AHA-1032 exhibited robust cyno cross reactivity (figure 2A) and had the most optimal profile, and therefore we selected this as our lead candidate (online supplemental figure 2B–D). One other complexity in developing an antibody against MICA is the polymorphic nature of the protein. There are more than 100 identified alleles and developing an antibody that binds to most of the alleles is an important criterion to maximize patient coverage.30 Notably, there are a few variants such MICA*008 (42.3%) that are more frequently observed in patient with cancer populations. We therefore cloned four such MICA variants and confirmed binding to AHA-1032. This provides a total coverage of as much as 61.2% of all the variants. Next, we compared the sequence homology of the alpha 3 domain of these four variants to the other remaining variants and found that they are greater than 95% similar, indicating that AHA-1032 can likely bind to most of the variants (figure 2B). The EC50 binding value of AHA-1032 to MICA overexpressing Raji cells was determined and found to correlate well with recombinant MICA binding (figure 2C).
We used AHA-1032 to produce our ADCC-enhanced antibody AHA-1031. To do so, we introduced mutations (S239D/A330L/I332E) to the CH2 domain of IgG-Fc as described previously23 to enhance IgG1-Fc binding to CD16a. Importantly, we did not observe a significant difference in MICA/B stabilization between the two antibodies (figure 2D). We next confirmed by biolayer interferometry (BLI) that the binding of AHA-1031 to the membrane proximal α3 MICA domain does not interfere with NKG2D binding to MICA. On the contrary, another antibody that binds to the α1 and α2 MICA domains, AHA-1678, blocks the binding of NKG2D to MICA (figure 2E). We next confirmed that increasing doses of AHA-1031 do not block NKG2D binding. We, therefore, incubated MC38 cells overexpressing MICA with either 6D4 or increasing doses of AHA-1031 and stained for NKG2D-Fc and analyzed by flow cytometry. We observed that staining with 6D4 impaired NKG2D-Fc binding whereas we observed binding of NKG2D-Fc with 10 µg/mL, 30 µg/mL, and 100 µg/mL of AHA-1031 (online supplemental figure 3A). We next examined whether blocking the NKG2D interaction with MICA leads to a reduction in target cell killing. We observed a significant reduction in primary NK cell killing of A375 cells in the presence of AHA-1031 at 1:1, 2:1, and 5:1 effector to target ratios but not at the high NK to tumor ratio 10:1 (online supplemental figure 3B). Taken together, these results demonstrate that the MICA/NKG2D axis is critical for antibody function.
Characterization of novel MICA/B antibodies AHA-1031 and AHA-1032 suggest engineered IgG1-Fc (AHA-1031) improved cell killing
Next, we wanted to confirm that AHA-1031 could effectively stabilize MICA and MICB specifically. Using ELISA assays that do not cross react, we observed that AHA-1031 reduced shed MICA and MICB in the media of A375 cells (figure 3A) and increased their expression on the cell surface (figure 3B). We next wanted to confirm that AHA-1031 has superior ADCC activity over AHA-1032. We therefore used a CD16+ Jurkat reporter cell assay with NFAT-mediated luciferase activation and observed a sevenfold increase in CD16-mediated NFAT activation compared with AHA-1032 (figure 3C). We further demonstrate a higher affinity of IgG1-Fc engineered AHA-1031 to CD16a by Gator Bio (BLI) when compared with AHA-1032. Briefly, biotinylated CD16a-158V (high-affinity variant) or CD16a-158F (low-affinity variant) were immobilized on a streptavidin sensor and dipped into AHA-1031 or AHA-1032. AHA-1031 binds to CD16a-158V and CD16a-158F with 17 nM and 27 nM KD which is comparable to the literature.31 Under the same conditions wild-type Fc containing AHA-1032 binds poorly to both variants of CD16a and is estimated to be about at least 10-fold lower affinity than binding to engineered IgG1-Fc (figure 3D). Another critical function of our antibody is its ability to perform antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP), another key aspect of immunity. To demonstrate this function with our antibody, we used Jurkat cells overexpressing CD32 H131 variant. Following engagement of stably expressing FcγRIIa-H131 with Fc region of AHA-1031 bound to A375 target cells resulted in intracellular signaling that turns on NFAT-RE-mediated luciferase activity as a readout for ADCP activity (online supplemental figure 3C). We note that 7C6 was also reported to have ADCP function in acute myeloid leukemia models.32
We next compared tumor cell killing by primary unstimulated NK cells in the presence of AHA-1031 or AHA-1032. We did not stimulate NK cells to reduce background killing. We observed that AHA-1031 has significantly increased tumor cell killing capacity compared with AHA-1032 even in the presence of 10 ng/mL soluble MICA in the media (figure 4A). Soluble MICA/B has been reported to decrease NK cell cytotoxic activity.33 We next performed an additional tumor cell killing assay with AHA-1031 where 100 ng/mL soluble MICA in the media significantly impaired NK cell killing (figure 4B). To our knowledge, 10 ng/mL represents the highest level of shed MICA reported in blood for metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer.34 In contrast, other shedding antigens such as MUC16, MUC-1, and CEACAM5 are typically shed at significantly higher levels (µg/mL) than MICA. This variance creates a “sink effect” posing a considerable challenge for antibodies targeting those tumors associated antigen to effectively reach the intended tumor site. This is most likely due to the sink effect as at lower concentrations of AHA-1031, 100 ng/mL of recombinant soluble MICA can compete with cell surface MICA for binding to AHA-1031. We notably observe variations in tumor cell lysis depending on the source of primary NK cell donors which is likely due to genotype variation. We observe in some cases AHA-1032 exhibits significantly lower cell killing compared with AHA-1031 at least under the conditions we performed these assays (online supplemental figure 3D).
Based on the data described, we propose the following mechanism of action for AHA-1031: It activates NK cells to mount a robust immune response via two main mechanisms: (1) anti-α3 MICA/B arm: blocks protease cleavage of MICA/B and restores immune surveillance (engagement of NKG2DL/NKG2D), and (2) engineered Fc: enhances ADCC function by promoting stronger binding to CD16a, thereby enhancing the ability of NK cells to target and kill cancer cells (figure 4C). These dual mechanisms collectively contribute to the potent immune response elicited by AHA-1031, making it a promising candidate for cancer immunotherapy.
Therapeutic efficacy and immune-mediated effects of AHA 1031 in KRAS LKB1 mutant xenograft models
With our in vitro results demonstrating antitumor activity and prevention of MICA/B shedding, we next evaluated the efficacy of our antibody in vivo. Given that the mouse NKG2D and FcgR receptors can bind functionally to human NKG2DLs and IgG1, respectively, we evaluated the in vivo efficacy of AHA-1032 and AHA-1031 in nude mice with MICA/B expressing human lung cancer cells (figure 5A). In H2030 xenografts we observed significantly decreased tumor growth with AHA-1032. We observed further improved efficacy with AHA-1031 including complete regression in two out of six mice (figure 5B). We detected no observable toxicity of our therapeutic through measurement of mouse body weight during and after treatment (online supplemental figure 4A). Treatment of human PBMCs with increasing doses of AHA-1031 did not result in a significant increase in the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines interferon-γ, interleukin (IL)-2, IL-4, and IL-17A further indicating safety in this setting (online supplemental figure 4B). Our results demonstrate the in vivo activity of both of our MICA/B antibodies and superior efficacy with AHA-1031.
To confirm efficacy in another model, we used the A549 model. We also noted significantly decreased tumor growth in AHA-1031 treated animals bearing A549 tumors as compared with vehicle control. However, we did not observe any complete responders in this experiment (figure 5C). This is likely because H2030 expresses higher levels of cell surface MICA/B. To determine the immune-modulatory effects of our therapeutic we isolated tumors from control and AHA-1031 treated animals bearing A549 tumors and performed flow cytometry analysis. Compared with control-treated animals, there were significantly increased lymphocyte infiltration (CD45/Live) and NK cell infiltration (NK/CD45). We also observed significantly increased activated NK cell populations through expression of key cytotoxic markers such as CD107a and granzyme B, and proliferation marker Ki-67 (figure 5D).
To determine whether MICA/B antibody is effective in a clinically relevant PDX model, we next utilized a KRAS G12A LKB1 mutant NSCLC PDX (LTL-657) in nude mice. KRAS G12A mutations are prevalent in NSCLC and found in nearly 7% of cases.35 We first isolated PDX tumors and profiled MICA/B expression through flow cytometry and detected moderate cell surface expression of MICA/B (figure 5E) which was further stabilized with increasing doses of the AHA-1031 (figure 5F). After confirmation of functionality, we implanted these tumors into mice and treated the mice with either vehicle or AHA-1031. We observed a significant decrease in tumor growth with AHA-1031 compared with vehicle control (figure 5G). Results from cell line and PDX models, demonstrate that AHA-1031 is effective in vivo across a range of MICA/B surface expression.
MICA/B stabilization and therapeutic efficacy of AHA-1031 across other cancer models
We next determined whether AHA-1031 can stabilize MICA/B on the cell surface of cell lines from different cancer types. AHA-1031 prevents shedding in lung cancer lines H2030, A549, Calu-3. Beyond lung cancer models, AHA-1031 stabilizes MICA/B expression in pancreatic (PANC1, Capan-2), colon (HCT116), ovarian (OVCAR3), and prostate cancer cell lines (22Rv1, PC3). These data therefore demonstrate the broad activity of AHA-1031 across cancer types (figure 6A,B and online supplemental figure 4C).
After confirming in vitro efficacy in various cancer models, we next determined therapeutic efficacy in another cancer type in vivo in the metastatic setting. We expressed MICA in B16F10 melanoma cells and injected B16F10-Lenti MICA cells intravenously into C57BL/6 mice to form lung metastatic tumors (figure 6C and 6D). The number of metastatic nodules in the lung were significantly less in AHA-1031 treated mice compared with vehicle-treated mice (figure 6E). These results demonstrate that AHA-1031 is a potential therapeutic strategy in lung and other MICA/B expressing cancers.
Discussion/conclusion
Here we demonstrate that our novel NK cell activating antibody, AHA-1031, shows potent MICA/B binding and ADCC activity resulting in the prevention of MICA/B ligand shedding and antitumor activity. We first demonstrate that KL mutant NSCLC cell lines have high cell surface expression of MICA/B. Patient blood sample analysis additionally shows that soluble MICA/B are detected across many tumor types. Our antibody exhibits strong binding properties that results in preventing MICA/B shedding across several solid tumor lines including lung, prostate, and pancreas. Using patient-derived models we show that AHA-1031 monotherapy significantly decreases tumor growth in vivo. In the tumor tissues of treated mice, activated NK cell populations are observed. Taken together, we show here our novel antibody design with an engineered IgG1-Fc region for enhanced ADCC activity elicits a therapeutic response in KL tumors.
Specifically, KL tumors have proved difficult to treat and have limited response to current immune-activating therapies.19 Multiple studies have shown that compared to other KRAS mutant tumors, KL tumors have far worse response to ICB therapy, which is currently the standard of care for patients with NSCLC.19 While we do not propose that this treatment is uniquely specific to KL tumors, since KL tumors do not benefit from other therapies, NK cell-modulating agents could be of significant benefit in this subtype. Future studies will investigate efficacy in other ICB-resistant tumors such as p53-deficient tumors.36
To date, NK cell-mediated therapies have lagged T-cell therapies across cancer types. Currently, the main therapeutics activating NK cells in clinical trials include cytokine stimulation such as IL-2 to increase NK/CD8 T cell activation and monoclonal antibodies such as monalizumab which binds to NK cell inhibitory receptor NKG2A.37 Chimeric antigen receptor NK cells have also been tested but have faced similar issues in solid tumors with immune cells not able to infiltrate the tumor.38 NK cells are particularly important in the lung and comprise 10-20% of all lymphocytes.39 In preclinical models of NSCLC, it was demonstrated that with the progression of Kras;p53 mutant NSCLC there was a significant decrease in NK cell functionality over time.2 However, our treatment can potentially overcome this by re-activating NK cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) through both preventing ligand shedding and ADCC-based mechanisms. Additionally, our antibody could potentially activate cytotoxic CD8 T cells as NKG2D signaling was shown to regulate T-cell activation, however, this was not the focus of this study.40 Currently clinically tested antibodies CLN-619 and DM919 both rely on WT human Ig1-Fc. However, our study demonstrates that substituting the WT IgG1-Fc with an engineered IgG1-Fc significantly enhances NK cell cytotoxicity.
In conclusion, we show that preventing MICA/B shedding and targeting MICA/B-expressing cancer cells is an effective therapeutic strategy in preclinical mouse models of KL mutant NSCLC. One limitation of our study is that we did not perform lung cancer model experiments in wild-type mice, which will be considered for future studies. Another limitation is that toxicity was not assessed in non-human primate models. The therapeutic potential of MICA/B antibody in targeting cancer cells with low baseline MICA/B expression is also of interest, particularly when combined with agents such as epigenetic modifiers or STING pathway inducers.9 41 MICA/B are widely expressed across NSCLC and other cancer types, making our therapeutic strategy widely applicable.
